February. Aunt Viorica’s New Year’s resolution: to learn to use her phone on her own. Andrei, who often comes round, has offered to give her lessons. The aunt speaks to him in Spanish, so she can practise too.
Very good, Aunt Viorica. This is the camera. To take a photo, press here, on the white circle.
Oh, my dear, it’s not that I don’t want to learn, but my fingers are too thick for these tiny screens.
Don’t worry, it happens to everyone. Look, you’ve already taken a photo. Of the ceiling, but it’s a photo.
(laughs) Delete it, delete it, I’m embarrassed.
No, I won’t delete it. You delete it: that’s how you learn. Hold your finger down on it and then press the bin.
I did it! And now how do I send a photo to Ana?
First open the messaging app. Look for Ana. Tap the paper clip and choose the photo. And send it.
Andrei, do you have those social media everyone talks about?
Yes, I post my drawings. I have about three thousand followers. But the fact that three thousand people follow you doesn’t mean you have three thousand friends.
How wise you are for nineteen. And aren’t you addicted, as they say on television?
A bit, I won’t lie to you. That’s why I disconnect on Sundays. No phone, no computer: just paper and pencil.
Then teach me to post a photo on those social media. I have an idea. But don’t tell Mihai yet.

When you add pronouns, the stress stays on the same syllable and an accent appears: BOrra → BÓrrala, enVÍa → enVÍala.
no-ES-keh: stress on ES, followed by a little pause: «No es que… [pause] no me guste».
bee-RAL (v = b), seh-gee-DOR (“gui” = “gee” with a hard g).
You use “no es que” to REJECT a possible explanation, then give the real explanation with “es que” (indicative) or “sino que” (indicative):
It’s not that I don’t want to; I just can’t.
It’s not that it’s hard; it’s that I don’t have time.
It’s not that it bothers me, but I’d rather you let me know.
In English we say “it’s not that it IS…” with the indicative; in Spanish, after “no es que”, the subjunctive always follows.
“El hecho de que” (the fact that) introduces a fact you COMMENT on. It’s usually used with the subjunctive, even when the fact is real:
It worries me that children spend so many hours in front of a screen.
With verbs of observation (es verdad, está claro) the fact is information → indicative. With “el hecho de que”, the focus is on the comment → subjunctive.

An article published on a Spanish newspaper’s website.
According to a recent survey, Spaniards look at their phones on average a hundred and fifty times a day. Eighty per cent admit they look at it before getting out of bed.
Experts point out that the problem isn’t technology itself. “It’s not that the phone is bad,” explains a psychologist, “it’s that we use it without thinking.”
What worries her most is the fact that many children get their first phone before the age of ten.
Her advice: choose a time of day to disconnect. “It’s essential that there are moments without screens, especially at the table.”

Aunt Viorica’s idea was simple. She wanted to tell the story of Vasile’s walnut tree. Not to the family, who already knew it, but to the world. “People nowadays have no patience with trees,” she had told Andrei. “Maybe if I tell them a story, they’ll find it again.”

For three Sundays in a row, Andrei broke his rule about disconnecting. He went to Viorica’s with his phone, a small tripod and a microphone borrowed from a friend at Fine Arts. They filmed Viorica sitting in her armchair, holding the old photo of the two soldiers that Mihai had lent her.

Viorica spoke in Romanian. Andrei added subtitles in Spanish and English, and Ana helped him check them. The video lasted seven minutes. At the end came the images from the garden: the moss-covered stump, the little walnut tree under the snow and Rosa Elena watering it with a watering can bigger than she was.

They posted it one Sunday evening, on Andrei’s account. Viorica chose the title: “What the earth gives back”. Then Andrei switched off his phone, as he did every Sunday, and went to bed without giving it another thought.
On Monday morning, when he switched it on, the phone wouldn’t stop vibrating. He had two hundred messages. The video already had forty thousand views.
By the afternoon there were two hundred thousand. By Tuesday, a million.

Andrei didn’t understand a thing. His drawings, which he worked on for weeks, usually got a few hundred likes. And now a video of an old woman speaking Romanian from an armchair had gone viral across half the world.

Comments came in every language. A woman in Argentina wrote that her grandfather had also buried something in the garden before he died and they had never looked for it; at the weekend she was going to dig. A man in Poland said his father had never talked about the war either. A little girl in Japan had drawn a walnut tree with a thousand paper cranes in its branches.
That drawing, they found out later, had been shared by Haruko Tanaka with all her friends in Kyoto. And one of those friends was the grandmother of an eight-year-old girl who drew beautifully.
On Wednesday Javier Ruiz called from Tokyo. He had seen the video, recognised the red crane in Rosa Elena’s pocket and wanted to write a feature.
On Thursday a Romanian TV channel called. On Friday, a Spanish radio station. Viorica, who two months earlier couldn’t take a photo, was now answering the phone by herself.
“It’s not that I like being famous,” she told Ana, very seriously. “But if I don’t answer, Elena does, and Elena tells them about her sugar-free cozonac.”

Mihai was the last to find out. He was at the hospital on a twenty-four-hour shift, with no time to look at his phone. When he finally came out, on Tuesday morning, a nurse came up to him in the corridor.
“Doctor, is the lady with the walnut tree your aunt? My mother cried three times watching the video.”
Mihai didn’t know what she was talking about. He opened his phone and saw forty missed calls. Half of them were from his mother.

At first he was a little annoyed. It’s not that he didn’t like the video: he thought it was beautiful. But nobody had asked him. It was his grandfather’s story, and suddenly a million strangers knew it.
That evening he went to see his aunt. Viorica was waiting for him with two cups of tea and the photo of the two soldiers on the table.

“I know you’re annoyed,” she said before he could open his mouth. “And you’re right: I should have asked you. But listen to me. Your grandfather could never tell what he’d been through. He kept it all inside for fifty years, and the only thing he left was a buried letter. The fact that a million people now know his name… Mihai, that’s what he wanted. For something good to come out of the earth.”

Mihai was silent. Then he picked up the photo and looked at the faces of the two young soldiers sitting on the rock. Underneath was another piece of paper: a printed message Andrei had brought Viorica that morning.

It was from a man in Porto, Portugal. His name was António, he was seventy-six and he had written in Spanish full of Portuguese words. He said his father, Ion Mărgărit, was Romanian. That he had arrived in Portugal after the war, without papers, and had never gone back to his country. And that as a young man, at the front, he always carried a small camera with which he photographed his comrades.

“I’ve seen the photo the lady is holding,” he wrote. “My father took it. I have the negative and another photo from the same day, in which all three of them are sitting on the same rock: Vasile, Gheorghe and him. My father talked about them every year on his birthday. He said they were his brothers.”
Mihai looked up from the letter. His hands were shaking.
“Auntie… Grandpa Gheorghe never told us about a third friend. Never. Not even when he gave us the photo.”
Viorica slowly nodded. For the first time all day, she wasn’t smiling.

“There are things the men from that war didn’t talk about,” she said. “Not even among themselves. And now that friend’s son has just found us thanks to a video. You see, Mihai. It’s not that social media is good or bad. But sometimes the earth gives things back in very strange ways. Tomorrow you’ll call Grandpa Gheorghe. He has to know before anyone else.”

That night, Mihai didn’t sleep. At three in the morning, Ana found him in the living room, in front of the computer, writing a reply to António. He had started it ten times. He had deleted it ten times.
“I don’t know what to say to him,” he confessed. “How do you start a letter to someone who knew your grandfather before you did?”
Ana sat down next to him, gently took the keyboard and typed a single sentence. Then she showed it to him.
“Dear António: when can we come and see you?”
Mihai read it twice. Then he pressed “send”, before he could change his mind. And for the first time all night, he laughed.

The next morning, Mihai called the village. Grandpa Gheorghe was ninety-four by now and could hardly hear on the phone, so he had to repeat the name three times: Ion. Ion Mărgărit. The one who took the photos.

At the other end of the line there was a silence so long that Mihai thought they’d been cut off. Then he heard a strange sound, like a cough. It took him a few seconds to understand that his grandfather was crying.

“I thought he was dead,” the old man said at last, his voice breaking. “He disappeared in forty-seven. One evening he was there, and the next morning he was gone. We never heard anything again. Vasile looked for him for years. I stopped looking. It’s not that I didn’t care, Mihai. But it hurt too much.”
“His son wants to meet you, Grandpa. He has a photo of the three of you.”
Silence again. And then, in a firmer voice, the voice of the soldier he had once been, Grandpa Gheorghe said:
“Tell him to come. To come quickly. At my age, you can’t wait for spring.”
Mihai hung up and stared at the phone for a moment. Then he opened the computer and wrote António a second message, much shorter than the first. This time he didn’t delete it even once.

It just said: “Dear António: my grandfather Gheorghe is waiting for you. He says to come quickly, because at his age you can’t wait for spring. We’ll pick you up at the airport. Bring the photo of the three of them.” He sent it at eight in the morning. By a quarter past eight, António had already replied with a single word in Romanian, the only one he had learned from his father as a child: “Vin” (I’m coming).
